summary: Re-verified all four CFG-01 / INFRA-1 / restore-stops-apps / tenant-relocate items the prior audits relied on, and they hold up: the rollback path resolves IMAGE_TAG from the dispatch input, re-pulls the immutable PREV_TAG image, checks out the matching commit (no current-code rebuild), and runs only forward-only `migrate:deploy` from the OLD code (no new migrations); backup.sh's off-host guard correctly queries the quoted Prisma column `"dbUrl"` and aborts loudly on relocated tenants; restore.sh stops api/worker/web and terminates backends before the DROP wave and validates archives first; tenant-relocate.ts's --drop-source now compares canonicalized endpoints + (server,dbName) tuple, resolves the source from audit beforeJson (never tenant.dbUrl), and requires --yes. Dockerfiles run as non-root (`USER node`), bake no secrets, and .dockerignore excludes **/.env; postgres-init.sql only creates extensions + a demo DB (no over-broad GRANTs); the admin-host gate keys off the real preserved Host header (not a spoofable X-Forwarded-Host), with the host firewall admitting only Cloudflare ranges. No committed .env.prod / secrets. Three real issues remain, none a clean RCE/cross-tenant: (1) HIGH — the deploy's post-`up` health gate curls Caddy's static always-200 /healthz, so a stack that comes up then crashes is reported healthy and auto-rollback never fires, undermining the documented "production never stays on a broken build" guarantee; (2) HIGH — no CPU/memory limits on any container in the single-host prod stack, so one OOM/runaway can take down Postgres and the whole cell; (3) MEDIUM — ensure-env.sh writes EMAIL_DRIVER=console into .env.prod, which env.ts accepts in production, re-introducing the REL-06 reset-token/PII-in-Docker-logs exposure the compose file's pass-through-empty default was written to prevent (intentional for the current no-email-provider trial, but the comment now overstates the gap is closed).

findings.title: Deploy health gate hits Caddy's static always-200 /healthz, not app health — a stack that crashes after `up` is reported healthy and auto-rollback never fires
findings.evidence: deploy.yml:321 `code="$(curl -sS -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}' --max-time 5 http://localhost/healthz ...)"` is the only post-deploy gate that triggers the `if: failure()` rollback step (deploy.yml:333-336). In the Caddyfile the plaintext :80 site answers that path with a static literal: `http:// { @probe path /healthz /readyz; handle @probe { respond "ok" 200 } ... }` (Caddyfile:115-119) — it never proxies to api or web. So the gate returns 200 whenever the Caddy container is up, independent of whether api/web/worker actually stayed healthy. The step's own comment (deploy.yml:305-313) claims it verifies 'the new code came up'. The real gate is `docker compose ... up -d` failing on `depends_on: condition: service_healthy` (deploy.yml:288), but that only checks health at the instant of `up`; a container that passes start_period then crash-loops (runtime error under load, flapping /readyz) is not caught here.
findings.impact: The documented DR guarantee 'production never stays on a broken build — the host is AUTOMATICALLY rolled back' (deploy.yml:148-152) does not hold for a deploy whose app comes up momentarily then fails. Operators get a green deploy and a down/degraded site, with no auto-rollback and no alert from this gate.
findings.fix: Probe real app health through the proxy instead of Caddy's literal: poll the api's readiness, e.g. `docker compose exec -T api wget -qO- http://localhost:3001/readyz` (the api container's own healthcheck target, compose:192) and the web's `/api/healthz`, on the host over the existing SSH session. Keep the static :80 /healthz only for the load-balancer liveness probe, not as the deploy success criterion.

adversarial.reason: The claim's central premise is refuted by the compose file. It asserts the Caddy static /healthz (Caddyfile:115-119, deploy.yml:321) is "the only post-deploy gate" and that `docker compose up -d` "only checks health at the instant of up." Both are false. In infra/compose/docker-compose.prod.yml the deploy actually gates on real application healthchecks via `depends_on: condition: service_healthy`: api (line 105-106 / 191-196) is probed at http://localhost:3001/readyz (15s interval, 8 retries, 30s start_period), web (line 103-104 / 224-229) at http://localhost:3000/api/healthz, and caddy (line 102-106) depends on BOTH being healthy. `up -d --force-recreate` (deploy.yml:288) blocks until those conditions are satisfied — it waits for the app readiness probes, it does not merely sample at the instant of up. So a deploy where api/web fail to come up exits non-zero, triggering the `if: failure()` rollback (deploy.yml:333-336). The DR guarantee (deploy.yml:149-152) therefore DOES hold for a build that fails to start. The author misread the gate: the Caddy /healthz poll (Wait for health step) is a secondary check whose stated purpose (deploy.yml:318-320) is to confirm the Caddy config RELOAD at line 299 took effect (new config = 200, stale config = 301-to-HTTPS), not to be the app-health gate. The only residual is the generic "container passes start_period then crash-loops under later production load" gap — but that is a universal property of every service_healthy-gated deploy, is not specific to the Caddy literal probe, and is explicitly scoped to uptime monitoring rather than the deploy gate by the code's own comment (deploy.yml:313). Runtime crashes are also mitigated by container healthchecks + restart:unless-stopped. Net: the impactful failure mode the claim describes (broken build reported healthy, no rollback) does not occur for a deploy that fails to come up; the narrow residual is a known, documented monitoring boundary, not a high-severity ops/DR defect.

findings.title: No CPU/memory limits on any container in the single-host prod stack — one OOM/runaway takes down Postgres and the entire cell
findings.evidence: `grep -n 'deploy:|resources:|limits:|mem_limit|cpus|memory:' docker-compose.prod.yml` returns nothing (exit 1). All seven services (caddy, migrate, api, web, worker, postgres, pgbouncer, redis) share the host with no containment; only `worker` has `stop_grace_period: 60s`. The compose header (lines 3-14) states this is a single host with app + data tiers co-located, and the alert rules anticipate the failure mode — HostLowMemory/HostSwapping/HostHighCPU (infra/monitoring/alerts.yml:30-72) — but nothing bounds a container. A bulk import, a runaway report query, or an api/worker memory leak can exhaust host RAM; the kernel OOM-killer or thrashing can take Postgres (the same box) with it.
findings.impact: A single tenant's heavy workload or one leaking process is a whole-cell availability and potential data-integrity risk (Postgres killed mid-write). On the documented single-host topology there is no blast-radius containment between the noisy workload and the database.
findings.fix: Add `deploy.resources.limits` (memory + cpus) and `mem_reservation` to at least api, web, worker (cap each well under host RAM), and a memory reservation/limit guardrail for postgres + redis. With plain `docker compose up` (not Swarm) use the `mem_limit`/`cpus`/`pids_limit` top-level keys, which compose honours. Also set Postgres `shared_buffers`/`work_mem` consistent with the chosen limit.

adversarial.reason: CONFIRMED. I independently verified infra/compose/docker-compose.prod.yml: no `deploy.resources`, `mem_limit`, `cpus`, `mem_reservation`, or `pids_limit` on ANY of the 7 services (caddy, migrate, api, web, worker, postgres, pgbouncer, redis). My grep for `deploy:|resources:|limits:|mem_limit|cpus|memory:|reservations|pids_limit` across infra/compose/ returned nothing (exit 1), matching the claim. Topology is confirmed single-host: the compose header (lines 1-22) and docs/deployment-hetzner.md describe one Hetzner box where Postgres shares the host with api/web/worker on private networks; deployment is plain `docker compose up` (NOT Swarm — confirmed via the guide and `restart: unless-stopped` usage), and `infra/deploy/fleet.yml` is just a host list with no resource config and no override compose file applies limits. Postgres is set only with `max_connections=200` and `shared_preload_libraries` — no `shared_buffers`/`work_mem` bound (docker-compose.prod.yml:275-283). The alert rules independently corroborate the anticipated failure mode: HostLowMemory (<12% RAM), HostSwapping (>50%), HostHighCPU (>85%, description literally says "Check for a bulk import/report") at infra/monitoring/alerts.yml:30-72, and the documented remediation is "grow the box" (Part 15) with only a 2G swapfile as cushion (deployment-hetzner.md:189-192) — i.e., no per-container blast-radius containment. The precondition (bulk import, runaway report, or an api/worker leak) is reachable in ordinary multi-tenant usage, so a noisy workload can drive the host OOM-killer/thrashing and take down co-located Postgres. I could NOT find any guard refuting this (no daemon ulimits, no systemd cgroup limits, no swarm deploy block). Notably Redis sets `--maxmemory-policy allkeys-lru` but no `--maxmemory`, so even that policy is inert — further confirming the gap. SEVERITY: correctly HIGH per the rubric (ops/DR with a reachable precondition), NOT critical: an OOM-kill of Postgres is crash-consistent (WAL+fsync) and recovers, so the claim's "potential data-integrity risk / Postgres killed mid-write" framing is overstated — this is a single-host availability/DR issue, not exploitable data corruption. With that one caveat trimmed, the finding is real, accurately evidenced (the author did not misread), and appropriately rated high.

findings.title: ensure-env.sh writes EMAIL_DRIVER=console into .env.prod, which env.ts accepts in production — re-opens the REL-06 reset-token/PII-in-Docker-logs exposure the compose default was written to close
findings.evidence: docker-compose.prod.yml:74 deliberately passes `EMAIL_DRIVER: ${EMAIL_DRIVER:-}` (empty when unset) with a comment (66-73) stating console 'writes password-reset token URLs (account-takeover material) and member PII into retained Docker logs' and that pass-through-empty forces env.ts to fail fast. But the deploy runs `bash scripts/ensure-env.sh --auto` (deploy.yml:259) which executes `ensure_default EMAIL_DRIVER console` (ensure-env.sh:98), writing `EMAIL_DRIVER=console` into /srv/libriant/.env.prod; the deploy then sources that file (deploy.yml:260) so compose's `${EMAIL_DRIVER:-}` resolves to `console`. env.ts then returns it verbatim with no prod guard: `if (raw === 'console' || raw === 'smtp' || raw === 'resend') return raw;` (env.ts:352). console-driver.ts:19-21 logs `to:`, `subj:` and the first 6 body lines at info level — reset/verification links sit at the top of those bodies — into json-file logs retained at 50m×5 (compose:90-95).
findings.impact: Once any real member exists, password-reset and email-verification token URLs plus member PII are written to host Docker logs readable by anyone with host/log access — account-takeover material. The compose comment's claim that the gap is closed is contradicted by ensure-env.sh. (Per project memory this console-only posture is intentional while no email provider is wired, so impact is currently bounded to the closed trial.)
findings.fix: Either stop defaulting EMAIL_DRIVER in ensure-env.sh (leave it unset so compose's pass-through-empty + env.ts fail-fast actually engages), or make env.ts refuse `console` when NODE_ENV=production unless an explicit ALLOW_CONSOLE_EMAIL escape hatch is set. Until a provider is wired, accept the risk explicitly and align the compose comment with reality.
